tagline.text: A 90 m freighter wreck in shallow Subic Bay

location.label: Location
location.text: Ilanin Bay on the east side of Subic Bay, off the Morong side of the Subic Bay Freeport Zone

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Clark International Airport (CRK) or Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL)

children.text: El Capitan is a freighter wreck about 90 m long, lying on its side on the sloping bottom of Ilanin Bay on the east side of Subic Bay. Its top begins at a depth of 4–5 m and the deepest point is about 20 m, so it is widely used as an introductory wreck dive.

El Capitan is a freighter wreck sunk in Subic Bay, on the western side of Luzon, and it is regarded as the most accessible wreck dive in Subic. It lies on its port (left) side on a shallow, sloping coral reef near the entrance to Ilanin Bay on the east side of the bay. Its upper side reaches a depth of about
and the deepest part is about

, so a diver with an Open Water certification can explore the whole ship without much strain. Many of the wrecks in Subic Bay have a clear draw, and El Capitan stands out as shallow and almost free of current, which is why it is often used for wreck diving courses.

The ship has a long history. It was launched in 1919 in Portland, Oregon, as the cargo ship Meriden. In 1923 it was sold to a lumber company in San Francisco, which renamed it El Capitan and used it in the West Coast lumber trade. In April 1942 the US Navy chartered and converted it, commissioning it as USS Majaba (AG-43). While on a supply run in support of the Guadalcanal campaign, it was hit by a torpedo off Lunga Point on 7 November 1942. The engine room was badly damaged but the ship did not sink; it was towed away and beached, and after repairs it served, with its engines removed, as a floating barracks and storage ship until the end of the war.

After the war the ship was moved to Subic Bay in the Philippines and declared a loss in March 1946, and it sank at Subic in July of that year. Wikipedia says it sank at its pier and was judged impossible to salvage, while some dive guides say it sank in a storm while anchored in Ilanin Bay, so the exact circumstances differ by source. Today the hull is described as about
long and about

wide. The superstructure is largely gone and part of the hull has collapsed, but the large cargo holds and openings in the hull remain open, making it fun to swim through. Some accounts also say the hull is covered with volcanic ash and sand from the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo.

Subic has several other wrecks as well, including the Spanish warship San Quentin, sunk in 1898 during the Spanish–American War; the cruiser USS New York, scuttled by the US Navy in 1941; the Japanese transport Oryoku Maru, bombed in 1944; and a landing ship (LST) that sank in 1946. El Capitan is the shallowest and easiest of these and is recommended as the first choice for wreck diving in Subic. Travelers without a diving certification cannot see it directly, so it is worth asking about a discovery dive or an Open Water course as well.
The top of the ship begins at
, so you can see the hull even near safety-stop depth. Even the deepest part is only about
, so air consumption is relatively slow and dives can last longer.

blocks.title: Swimming through big holds and hull openings

children.text: The front of the hull is wide open, so you can slowly enter the large cargo holds and the crew quarters. Shafts of sunlight streaming through the openings are the signature scene of this site, and going deeper inside the hull requires specialist training.

blocks.title: Sheltered bay with almost no current

children.text: It lies in a protected area on the east side of Subic Bay, so there is almost no current and the waves are small. It suits people trying wreck diving for the first time and divers practicing buoyancy control.

Built in 1919, it has served as a lumber carrier, a Navy supply ship, a torpedo victim and a storage ship, so it is far more interesting if you listen to your guide. Each dive center explains the ship's structure in its pre-dive briefing.

The hull and the surrounding slope are described as home to glassfish, tangs, wrasses, gobies, spotted sweetlips, lobsters, crabs and clownfish. The number and variety of animals change with the season and the day.
Because it is shallow and has no current, it is often used for wreck specialty courses and training after Open Water. Training also teaches how far you can safely go inside the ship.

blocks.title: A day trip combined with other wrecks

children.text: Boats from Subic dive centers usually leave early in the morning and visit two or three sites. A common plan is to make El Capitan the first dive and continue to other wrecks such as San Quentin. The schedule varies with the center and the weather.

items.title: Half-day dive
items.subtitle: From the Subic dive center to El Capitan

children.text: Meet at a dive center inside the Subic Freeport Zone, fit your gear and register. You will need to show your certification card and recent dive records, so bring them.
Many centers list this as the boat departure time. El Capitan is a short boat ride away, so seasickness is not a big worry.

In the pre-dive briefing you agree on the shape of the hull, the maximum depth, the openings you can enter and when to check your air. Because the top is shallow, the usual route starts at the top of the ship and gradually descends.
Descend, follow the deck, pass through the large cargo hold and exit through an opening in the hull. A full lap with the guide usually takes about
40–50 minutes
After a surface interval, either continue to another site such as San Quentin for a second dive, or return to the center, rinse your gear and finish.

The number and order of dives change on site depending on weather, currents and other groups' schedules. If you are flying, you must follow the rules on the interval between your last dive and the flight, so talk to the center beforehand.

items.title: Full day
items.subtitle: Two or three wrecks plus time in the Freeport

children.text: Have breakfast at your lodging in the Freeport and head to the dive center.
Make your first dive at El Capitan. Start in the shallows and ease into it.
Have lunch at a restaurant near the center or at your lodging and rest.
Make a second dive at another wreck or reef-slope site, then finish for the day.
Finish with a walk along the Subic Bay waterfront or some duty-free shopping.
This schedule is an example. Follow the boat timetable set by your dive center.
Victory Liner buses to Olongapo run frequently from early morning until evening from the Cubao, Pasay, Sampaloc and Caloocan terminals in Manila. The trip usually takes
2–4 hours
From the Olongapo terminal, take a jeepney or taxi into the Subic Bay Freeport Zone and go to your dive center. You must show ID at the Freeport entrance, and fees change, so confirm them on site.
Bus schedules and fares can change, so check at the terminal.

items.title: From Manila by car or rental car

children.text: The usual route is NLEX and SCTEX to the Subic toll gate, which takes about
2–3 hours
. Tolls from Manila (Balintawak) to Subic are about ₱600 each way (2026 sources range from ₱550 to ₱850), so check with Easytrip or your entry point.
Speed limits and traffic rules are strict inside the Freeport Zone, so follow the signs.
From Clark International Airport to Subic is about
1–1.5 hours
by car using a private transfer service. The cost is reported at about ₱2,500~3,500, but it varies with the number of people and vehicle type, so check in advance.

items.title: Dive center and getting to the site

children.text: El Capitan is near the entrance of Ilanin Bay, a short boat ride from the dive center. It is not a place where ordinary travelers rent their own boat, so booking a dive center trip is the norm.

The dry season from November to May is best for diving in Subic, and water is often clearest from February to May. Because El Capitan is inside the sheltered bay, dives are often possible even in shoulder months such as June and October, but rain can make visibility worse.
In the rainy season from July to September, typhoons and wind sometimes cancel boat trips. Water temperature is about
all year, so a 3 mm wetsuit is enough for most people, and some divers choose 5 mm for several dives a day.

items.label: Accommodation
items.note: From budget rooms to beach resorts

Lodging is split between the Subic Bay Freeport Zone, Olongapo and the Barretto beach area. If diving is the goal, lodging close to the centers in the Freeport is the most convenient, while Olongapo and Barretto have guesthouses and budget-to-mid-range hotels if you want to save money. Many dive centers also run or partner with lodging, so ask when you book.

Meals are found at waterfront restaurants in the Freeport and at Barretto beach restaurants. There are both Korean and Filipino restaurants, and after diving it is best to eat lightly and drink plenty of water. Planning at least a day of rest before flying is also better for decompression safety.
Bring your certification card and logbook. The center checks your certification level and the date of your last dive.
El Capitan is shallow and relatively easy, but visibility inside the ship can drop, so do not lose your guide.
Kicking up sediment from the bottom makes visibility drop quickly. Keep neutral buoyancy and short fin kicks over the hull.
Bring a dive light to see the life inside the cargo holds better. Ask whether the center can rent you one.
Morning boats often have lighter wind and fewer people. Book by the day before.
When entering the wreck, go only as far as you can still see the exit. Going deeper inside requires specialist training and gear.
Follow the center's rules on rest time before flying after diving.
Visibility is reported at about 5–15 m depending on the day and location. Keep your expectations modest and enjoy the shape and atmosphere of the hull.
Inside the wreck visibility drops and there are rusty steel structures that are dangerous. Do not go deep without the proper certification and gear.
Wreck structures are sharp and fragile and can cut you if you grab them without gloves. Avoid touching them as much as possible.
Visibility inside the bay can be poor and there is boat traffic, so look around when you surface.
Follow the center's rules and your guide's instructions. Do not find your own boat or dive at unauthorized sites.
In the rainy season, check typhoon news and leave spare days in case boat trips are canceled.
Anchoring on the ship or hull, or taking artifacts away, is prohibited.
You can see the whole bay where El Capitan lies, with Freeport Zone lodging, restaurants, a marine theme park and jungle activities. It is within about
10–20 minutes
by car.
North of Subic are small islands in Zambales that pair well with beaches and snorkeling. Check travel times locally.
This is the volcano whose 1991 eruption is the source of the ash covering El Capitan's hull, and you can trek to the caldera lake.
Clark, about
1–1.5 hours
from Subic by car, has an international airport and is a hub if you fly.
